metric.why: Facilities strand capacity when racks are provisioned against nameplate ratings nobody ever draws, and trip breakers when AI training loads spike synchronously. Circuit-level telemetry is how both failure modes are caught.
metric.target: Common practice derates circuits to 80 percent of breaker rating for continuous load, per US electrical code.
metric.definition: Per-circuit measurement of how much of each breaker's rated capacity is in use, tracked continuously and at peak.

reading.body:
Breaker-level load monitoring is the most direct signal a data center has of whether its power infrastructure is being used or abused, catching both stranded capacity and dangerous spike conditions before either wastes money or trips a circuit.

The 80-percent derating rule built into US electrical code creates a practical ceiling: continuous loads must stay below that threshold, which means the gap between nameplate ratings and real draw is not slack, it is required headroom. AI training workloads complicate this because they can spike synchronously across many racks at once, pushing instantaneous draw toward or past that ceiling in ways that steady-state averages will never reveal. Circuit-level telemetry, tracked continuously and at peak, is what makes the difference between catching that condition and discovering it through a tripped breaker.

The data describes the metric and its rationale but does not supply measured values, utilization distributions, or comparisons across facility types. It does not address how breaker-level data is aggregated into facility-wide decisions, or how it relates to upstream grid connections. The sibling metrics, PUE, DCiE, and power density per rack, operate at different granularities, and this metric sits closer to the physical circuit than any of them.
